quotes.quote: Laws start as bills – a written proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law.
a bill must be agreed to in identical form by both the Senate and House of Representatives
Ideas for new laws can come from many different places:
A government department may tell its minister about a problem that needs fixing.
Political parties have their own ideas about how Australia should be governed.
They can speak to members of parliament with suggestions for bills.
If the issue requires action, the committee may suggest that a bill be introduced.
Most bills are introduced by government ministers.
Other members of parliament can introduce their own bills, known as private members' or private senators' bills.
starts on the date included in the law or, if no date is given, 28 days after Royal Assent.
It can take months or even years for a bill to become law but most bills take 2 to 3 months.
Around 200 bills are introduced into Parliament each year
Either house of Parliament can send a bill to a committee for detailed examination.
A committee might suggest changes to a bill or make other recommendations for the Houses to consider.
it is sent to the other house – in this case, the Senate – where a similar process is followed.
One of the main roles of the Australian Parliament is to make laws for the people of Australia.

sources.title: The usual path of a bill

quotes.quote: the Senate may refer the text of the bill to a Senate committee for inquiry (this can happen while the bill is in the House).
Consideration in detail (optional stage) – members discuss the bill in detail, including any changes to the bill
3rd reading – members vote on the bill in its final form the bill is passed in the House of Representatives and sent to the Senate.
In the Senate a bill goes through the following stages:
Amendments to bills are most often considered during committee of the whole in the Senate or consideration in detail in the House of Representatives.
can speak about each amendment and vote for or against each amendment.
Any member of parliament can suggest an amendment to a bill. This is called 'moving an amendment'.
An amendment must be submitted in writing to the Clerk of the Senate or House.
The Clerk then distributes copies so that everyone can read the amendment
Amendments can be introduced in either the Senate or the House of Representatives, and must be agreed to by both.
Amendments can be introduced in either the Senate or the House of Representatives, and must be agreed to by both.
These laws provide a general framework and don’t include details about when, where and how the laws might be applied.
give the power to make decisions about the details of these complex laws to the person or group with expert knowledge
There are different types of delegated law including determinations, regulations, ordinances and orders.
Delegated law has the same power as a law made by the Australian Parliament.
It can be made and changed without having to be debated and passed by the Parliament.
Each delegated law must be listed on a public register.
Then it must be presented to Parliament within 6 sitting days.
Within 15 sitting days, a member of parliament must request the Senate or House of Representatives overrule the delegated law.
The Senate or House of Representatives have 15 sitting days to discuss the delegated law and make a decision.
If there is no discussion or no decision is made, the delegated law is overruled.
Some delegated law cannot be overruled.
A division is a formal recorded vote where members of Parliament divide into 2 groups to vote for or against a proposal.
The Australian Parliament makes decisions on proposed laws and other issues by a majority vote.
Most decisions of the Parliament are made by voting ‘on the voices’.
The division bells usually ring for 4 minutes.
Once the bells have stopped, the doors are locked.
Members of parliament who arrive after the bells stop are not allowed to enter.
asks those who want to vote for the proposal to move to the right side of their chair
and those voting against to move to the left.
Votes are counted and the names of those voting are recorded.
The result is announced by the Presiding Officer.
the Speaker of the House does not vote unless the result is a tie.
The President of the Senate may always vote along with other senators.
This ensures all the states have equal representation when votes are taken in the Senate.
If there is a tied vote in the Senate, the question is not agreed to
Members of parliamentary parties usually vote as a team in Parliament, with all party members voting the same way.
parties often have rules about voting as a team.
are responsible for making sure party members know how to vote
working together gives members more power than acting alone
Crossing the floor is when a member of parliament votes against the rest of their party during a division – a formal vote.
they walk across or ‘cross’ the floor to sit opposite the other members of their team.
Crossing the floor is rare and usually only happens after careful consideration.
they strongly agree or disagree with a particular policy or decision
they believe a different outcome would be better for the people in their state, territory or electorate
the issue is a matter of personal values or conscience.
Crossing the floor may affect the support or opportunities a member receives within their party
In a free vote – sometimes called a conscience vote – members of parliament are not required to vote with their party.
Each parliamentary party decides when its members are allowed a free vote.
Between 1950 and 2021, only 43 votes on bills and other issues in the Parliament were decided by a free vote.
Free votes have mostly been used to decide issues such as euthanasia, stem cell research or same-sex marriage.
They are usually made up of 6 to 10 members of parliament and have a mix of government and non-government members.
Individuals and groups are invited to send submissions – opinions and proposals – to committees.
they invite people or groups to appear at hearings to provide more information or answer questions from committee members.
After the hearings are finished, the committee writes a report which is presented to Parliament.
Committees investigate issues and bills in detail.
Members of parliament might use the report to help them decide how they will vote on a bill or to develop bills or amendments
The Budget is a collection of bills – proposed laws – called appropriation bills.
A party whip is a member of Parliament chosen by their political party to help keep their party organised
They help the party work as a team.
Smaller parties may only have a whip where they have members or choose not to have a whip.
organising party members to make sure they attend and vote together during divisions
counting and recording the votes in a division
so numbers between the government and opposition stay balanced if members are away.
major parties usually have a chief whip and 2 deputy whips.

the Parliament is made up of the Monarch, represented by the Governor-General, and two houses of Parliament: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
there is approximately the same number of voters living in each electorate.
There are 76 senators. Each state is represented by 12 senators, and the Northern Territory and Australian Capital Territory are represented by 2 senators each.
A senator is someone who has been elected to represent their state or territory in the Senate.
State senators are elected for a period of 6 years
every 3 years half of the state senators are up for re-election

sources.title: Members of the House of Representatives (fact sheet)

quotes.quote: There are 150 members. Each represents a different electorate.
Members are elected to the House of Representatives at least every 3 years.
The Prime Minister of Australia is the leader of the Australian Government.
The people of Australia do not vote for the Prime Minister.
the Prime Minister is chosen by a vote of the members of the party in government.
By convention – tradition – the Prime Minister is always a member of the House of Representatives, not a senator.
The role of Prime Minister is not mentioned in the Australian Constitution.
selecting members of the government to be ministers
It includes the Prime Minister and about 20 ministers who are part of the executive government.
Cabinet meets on a regular basis, often weekly.
Cabinet's role is to develop government policy and make decisions about national issues.
Once Cabinet has made a decision, all Cabinet ministers are expected to support the decision publicly.
The Prime Minister chooses experienced and knowledgeable government members to be ministers
Ministers are members of the Australian Government who have been given an area of responsibility for how Australia is run.
This area of responsibility is known as a portfolio. Examples of ministerial portfolios include: health environment transport defence
There are usually about 20 ministers in the House of Representatives and 10 in the Senate.
They are chosen by the Leader of the Opposition. Each shadow minister concentrates on the work of a particular minister and government department.
They also act as the opposition spokesperson for the area they are assigned.

quotes.quote: call on members when it is their turn to speak
conduct votes in the House and announce the results
After a federal election, members of the House of Representatives vote to choose the Speaker.
maintain order and issue warnings if senators have broken the rules
They are elected by fellow senators to run the meetings of the Senate.
No Governor-General has ever refused to give Royal Assent to a bill
The Governor-General is the King’s representative in Australia.
The Governor-General is appointed by the King on the recommendation of the Prime Minister.
It is an established convention that the Governor-General follows the advice of the Government
One of their most important jobs is giving Royal Assent to bills – proposed laws – passed by the Senate and House of Representatives.
An independent is a member of the Australian Parliament who does not belong to a political party.
The government often does not have a majority in the Senate.
Independent and minor party senators can have the balance of power – their vote can decide if a bill is passed or fails.
does not have enough members in the House of Representatives to be the government or the opposition.
The opposition is the largest party – or coalition of parties – that does not have the support of the majority of members
The opposition is sometimes called the alternative government because it could form government if it was to win the support of the majority of members.
The opposition has an important role in keeping the government accountable to the Australian Parliament.
providing alternatives to government policies.
The government may or may not hold the majority of seats in the Senate.
The Senate again rejects or fails to pass the bill, or passes the same bill with amendments to which the House will not agree.
There have been 7 double dissolutions of the Australian Parliament: 1914, 1951, 1974, 1975, 1983, 1987 and 2016.
the Governor-General may call a joint sitting of all senators and members of the House of Representatives.
At a joint sitting, all senators and members vote together on the bill or bills.
There has only been one joint sitting of the Australian Parliament.
In 1974, the 6 bills that had triggered a double dissolution were reintroduced into Parliament
The signing of a bill by the Governor-General, which is the final step in making a bill into a law.
in which the bill is introduced and the title of the bill is read for the first time.

A stage in the passage of a bill through the Senate, in which senators discuss the bill in detail, including any suggested changes.
in which members of parliament vote on the bill in its final form.
A proposed law that introduces a tax or suggests spending money for a particular purpose.
Rules or regulations made by a government minister, executive office-holder or government department using power that is given to them by the Parliament.
A meeting of a house of parliament.
The top-level parliamentary officer in the Senate or the House of Representatives.
A special proclamation to formally close a session of the Parliament, used before a dissolution of the House of Representatives
A geographical area represented by a member of parliament, also referred to as a seat.
A person elected to the House of Representatives, also referred to as an MP.
the party, or coalition of parties, with the support of the majority of members in the House of Representatives.
An agreement between two or more parliamentary parties to create a bigger group and strengthen their position.
The seats in the Senate or the House of Representatives occupied by minor parties and/or independents.
In the Senate called the President and in the House of Representatives called the Speaker.
The organisation responsible for running national elections and referendums.

sources.title: Does the Federation Chamber have a part in the law making process?

quotes.quote: The Federation Chamber is the second meeting place of the House of Representatives and can operate at the same time as the House.
All members of the House can attend the Federation Chamber.
debating bills on which there is expected to be agreement
although divisions – formal recorded votes – cannot be taken there.
All decisions made in the Federation Chamber need to be confirmed by the House of Representatives.

sources.title: What happens to a law that is not passed by one of the houses?

quotes.quote: If one of the houses doesn't pass a bill – a proposal for a new law – then it cannot become a law.
pass the bill again and send it back to the second house
change the bill so the second house will be more likely to pass it
lay the bill aside (not go forward with the bill).
the Prime Minister can ask the Governor-General to call an election for all the seats in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

sources.title: What does it mean when members say "I move that this bill now be read a second time"?

quotes.quote: To pass through the Senate or House of Representatives, the title of the bill must be read out 3 times by the Clerk.
Each time the Clerk reads the title of the bill it signals the bill has passed a different stage.
When a member of parliament says ‘I move that this bill now be read a second time’
the member or senator (usually a minister responsible for the bill) moves a motion – asks – that it be read a second time.
members of parliament discuss the principle or main idea of the bill and can explain why they support or oppose the bill.
If the vote passes, it signals that senators or members agree with the main idea of the bill
The bill can then progress through the next stages, including discussion of amendments – changes – to the bill.

sources.title: How many votes are needed for a bill to pass the House of Representatives and the Senate?

quotes.quote: asks members of parliament to cast their vote for or against the bill by saying 'aye' or 'no'.
The President or Speaker decides which response has more support and announces the result.
If the result is challenged by more than one member of parliament, a division is held.
In the Senate, at least 19 senators (one quarter of the total number of senators) must vote in a division for it to count.
In the House, 30 members must be present (one fifth of the total number of members).

the Senate and House of Representatives spend most of their time considering government business
the government usually has the majority in the House of Representatives, so a private bill will only succeed if the government supports it.

quotes.quote: signs a document, known as a ‘message’, addressed to the President of the Senate, requesting the Senate’s ‘concurrence’ – agreement – with the bill.
decide to immediately debate the bill, send it to a committee for closer examination or schedule debate on the bill for a later day.

send the bill back to the Parliament with suggestions for amendments – changes.

quotes.quote: A bill – proposed law – is introduced in the house where the person responsible for it sits.
Most ministers are members of the House, so most bills are introduced there.
money and taxation bills must be introduced in the House of Representatives.

quotes.quote: If the majority agree to an amendment, the bill is changed.
Independent, minor party and opposition members are more likely to suggest amendments. This is because most bills introduced to Parliament are government bills
